title: Fluency
description: Accuracy is saying it right. Fluency is saying it without stopping to build every sentence from scratch. On a client call, nobody waits while you mentally conjugate verbs

lessons.title: The golden rule: never correct during a fluency task

steps.body: Accuracy is saying it right. Fluency is saying it *without stopping to build every sentence from scratch*. On a client call, nobody waits while you mentally conjugate verbs — pauses read as uncertainty, and uncertainty loses work. The research is clear on the mechanism: fluency and accuracy compete for the same attention (Skehan's trade-off), so we train them *separately* — fluency tasks with zero correction, accuracy tasks with full correction — and then integrate them by repeating tasks.

Two modes. Never mix them.

- **Fluency mode:** timed retell, free talk, role-play. Goal: keep going. Mistakes are not just allowed — they're *invisible* until the task ends. If you stop to fix an article, you've left fluency mode and the drill is wasted.
- **Accuracy mode:** recorded, transcribed, corrected (Modules 2–3 drills). Goal: fix it.

After a fluency task, you MAY do an accuracy pass on the recording. That's the integration: *do it fluent → get feedback → redo it better* (task repetition — the evidence says this is what actually merges fluency and accuracy).

steps.title: The retell ladder
steps.prompt: Listen to a 2-minute clip (your narrow-input source). Then retell it in your own words: 90 seconds → 60 seconds → 45 seconds. Same content, shrinking time. No notes on round 1; keywords only on rounds 2–3. Fluency mode: NO correction, NO stopping. Record all three; compare round 1 vs round 3 — round 3 is always smoother. That's task repetition working.
steps.tip: Fluency mode: no stopping, no mid-sentence correcting.

steps.body: One minute of planning before speaking improves accuracy dramatically; more than a few minutes adds almost nothing. For client calls, this is a superpower: before the call, rehearse answers to the 5 predictable questions (who are you, what do you do, how would you approach this, what's your timeline, what's your price). Planned performance is the legal cheat code — you sound fluent AND accurate because you did the accuracy work *before* the pressure.

steps.heading: How to plan in 60 seconds
steps.body: jot 3–4 keyword bullets (NOT full sentences — full sentences turn into reading). Then speak from the bullets.

steps.title: Plan it, say it, redo it
steps.prompt: Client question: "How would you approach building a sales dashboard for a clothing shop?" Take exactly 60 seconds to write 4 keyword bullets. Speak for 90 seconds. Then: listen to your recording, note 2 errors, and redo the answer once. The redo is where fluency + accuracy fuse.
steps.tip: Fluency mode: no stopping, no mid-sentence correcting.

steps.body: The JALT study on Urdu-L1 learners found it plainly: *"My mind follows Urdu word order automatically."* As long as you compose in Urdu then translate, you'll be slow forever. Retraining:

1. **Narrate your day in English, silently.** *"I'm making chai. The water is boiling. I'll check my phone after this."* Start with present actions — no translation needed because you're describing, not converting.
2. **Name 10 things around you in English** every morning. Builds direct concept→English links.
3. **When stuck on a word mid-sentence, describe around it** (circumlocution): don't freeze searching for "dashboard" — say *"the page that shows your sales numbers."* Clients respect this; freezing they don't.
4. **Dream in English?** Not required. But the day you catch yourself thinking *"I need to buy milk"* instead of *"doodh lena hai"* — that's the switch flipping.

steps.title: Filler detox
steps.prompt: Explain "What is Python?" to an imaginary shopkeeper in 60 seconds. Record. Count your fillers (umm, matlab, you know, like). Now re-record with the replacement table taped in front of you. Target: under 3 fillers. Repeat weekly with a new topic (SQL, mean vs median, machine learning — the Feynman bank from your communication program works here).
steps.tip: Fluency mode: no stopping, no mid-sentence correcting.

steps.body:
Fillers aren't evil — natives use "um" too. But *matlab*, *you know*, and long *ummm*s signal "I'm translating right now." Replace, don't just remove:

Instead of... · Say... (or do...)
matlab... · "What I mean is..."
you know (every sentence) · delete it, or "as you know" (once per call max)
ummm (long) · silent pause — pauses sound confident, umms sound lost
like (filler) · "for example"
Freezing on a word · describe around it (Lesson 4.3.3)

steps.heading: The pause trick
steps.body: when you need thinking time, say *"That's a good question — let me think for a second."* You've bought 5 seconds and sounded thoughtful doing it.

One focused week per month. Same drill every day, 20 minutes. Pick ONE per sprint:

- **Sprint A — Retell week:** one new 2-minute clip per day, retell ladder (90s → 60s → 45s).
- **Sprint B — Question week:** answer 5 bank questions per day (Module 5, Lesson 5.4) with 60-second planning, recorded.
- **Sprint C — Narration week:** narrate your entire day in English, silently, from waking to sleeping. Every action, every plan. When you catch yourself translating — stop, describe instead.

Rules for sprint weeks: fluency mode ONLY (no correction during tasks). Do your accuracy pass on Sunday using the week's recordings. One sprint per month is enough — more burns you out, fewer lets fluency rust.

steps.title: 30-second news sprint
steps.prompt: Read one short news paragraph. You have 30 seconds to retell it — SVO sentences only, no stopping. Do it 3× back-to-back, faster each time. This builds automaticity under pressure: the exact skill a live call demands.
steps.tip: Fluency mode: no stopping, no mid-sentence correcting.

steps.title: Quiz — Fluency

questions.prompt: Combine into one smooth sentence using "get back to":
options: "I will get back you to tomorrow."
"I will get back to you tomorrow."
questions.explanation: I will get back to you tomorrow. ("get back to" is one unbreakable chunk)

questions.prompt: "I am writing this email to inform you about the delay." (aim: under 12 words)
questions.sample: Sample: "Quick update — I'm running a little behind, but Thursday is locked in."
questions.explanation: Sample: "Quick update — I'm running a little behind, but Thursday is locked in."

questions.wrong: Um, so I, like, started the project yesterday.
questions.answer: I started the project yesterday. (zero fillers — pause silently instead)
questions.explanation: I started the project yesterday. (zero fillers — pause silently instead)

questions.prompt: Put this delay email in order:
questions.sample: b-a-d-c — greeting → reason → what you're doing now → new date
questions.explanation: greeting → reason → what you're doing now → new date

questions.prompt: Client: "Can you do it cheaper?" Best reply?
options: "I can adjust the scope to fit your budget."
questions.explanation: never just drop price; trade scope

questions.prompt:
You: "___"
   Client: "Sounds good, let's start Monday."
questions.sample: Sample: "I can start Monday. I'll send a short plan with milestones, and your first update lands Wednesday."
questions.explanation: Sample: "I can start Monday. I'll send a short plan with milestones, and your first update lands Wednesday."

questions.sample: Sample: "Could you send the requirements when you get a chance? I'll start as soon as they arrive."
questions.explanation: Sample: "Could you send the requirements when you get a chance? I'll start as soon as they arrive."

options: "I usually take a 30% advance before starting — is that okay?"
questions.explanation: states the policy as normal process, asks permission

questions.sample: Do you need the report by Friday?
questions.explanation: Do you need the report by Friday?

questions.prompt:
Write the FIRST line (a hook) of a 60-second talk about your week.
---
questions.sample: Sample: "This week I finally finished something I'd been avoiding for a month." (energy, not "Um, so this week…")
questions.explanation: Sample: "This week I finally finished something I'd been avoiding for a month." (energy, not "Um, so this week…")

steps.rule: 8/10 to move on. Answer first, then learn from the misses.

steps.heading: Can-do statements
steps.body:
- [ ] I can retell a 2-minute clip in 60 seconds without long pauses
- [ ] I plan with keyword bullets (60 sec) before any important speaking
- [ ] I can narrate my daily routine in English without translating from Urdu
- [ ] My filler count is under 3 per minute (measured on recordings)
- [ ] When I forget a word, I describe around it instead of freezing

steps.heading: Mini-test
steps.body: Record a 2-minute answer to *"Tell me about yourself and what you're learning."* Score: pauses over 3 seconds (count them — target ≤2), fillers (target ≤5), and one thing that improved vs your Module 0 placement recording.

steps.heading: Re-entry note
steps.body:
Fluency rusts fast. Back after a break? Three days of Drill 4.1 before anything else — retelling rebuilds flow quicker than any other drill.

🌊 **Badge earned: Flow State** — you can now keep talking. Next: saying the right things to the right people.
